name: Zane Novak

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Zane. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me both what you'd say in public and what you really think. Is that all right?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Sure, that works. I've done a couple of these surveys before, but never a proper conversation, so let's see.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm at Millbrook Health Centre, a group clinic of nine doctors in a market town. I start at half eight, see about twenty-eight patients a day in fifteen-minute slots, and do phone calls and repeat prescriptions in the gaps. Lots of chest infections, blood pressure checks, worried parents and older people with five conditions at once. Twice a week I use the AI note-taker the clinic is trialling, mostly when I'm running late. The best bit is the regulars, the farmer who brings me eggs at Easter. The worst bit is the inbox, which never empties.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's about what I expected. The note-taker saves me maybe twenty minutes on a busy day, which is nice, and that's it. I'd probably joke about it at lunch with the nurses.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it means things carry on, and that's fine with me. The job is busy but secure, the pay is decent, and there are a few clinics within driving distance if I ever wanted to move. I'm not losing sleep.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on as I am and keep using the note-taker on the late days. I'd keep saving toward a flat with my partner Ines, maybe a deposit in two or three years. And I'd keep going to the local doctors' association meetings, because the workload issue doesn't go away just because AI fizzled.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty calm, if I'm honest. A bit flat, like the future was oversold.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do with the twenty minutes the note-taker saves?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Leave on time, mostly. Ines and I cook together on Wednesdays and I've missed about half of them this year. Twenty minutes is the difference between making it home for Wednesday dinner or not.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything in that picture that does worry you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The workload, a bit. Two of our older doctors retire next year and we haven't found anyone yet. If they don't get replaced, my list grows, but that's a staffing story, not an AI one.

say: I'd say AI turned out about **as expected** and saves a little time.
I'd joke at lunch that the **note-taker** is the only win.
think: I think my job stays **busy but secure**, with decent pay.
There are **other clinics** nearby if I ever wanted to move.
do: Keep using the **note-taker** on late days to leave on time.
Keep saving for a **flat deposit** in two or three years.
Keep attending the **doctors' association** meetings on workload.
feel: He feels **calm** and a little **flat**, as if the future was oversold.
S0.quote: Twenty minutes is the difference between making it home for Wednesday dinner or not.
fieldNote: His work and money feel **secure**, so AI Plateau barely touches him.
His only worry is **two retirements** next year that could grow his list.
He uses AI **practically**, for time, not as a belief system.

steps.text: Keep using the clinic's note-taker on late days
Save each month toward a flat deposit with his partner
Carry on seeing his patient list at Millbrook as normal

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a big change and we should shape it, not just let it happen. I'd want the doctors' association pushing for patient safety rules and for staff to share in any time saved. Online I'd probably share articles about it, but I wouldn't rant.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think it's mostly good for me in the short run. The letters, the referrals, the coding of diagnoses, that's the stuff I hate. But I'd worry the clinic owners use the saved time to cut the number of doctors, and I'm the most junior salaried one after the trainees.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask to be on the group that picks the clinic's AI tools, once I saw it working at other clinics first. I'd do the short online course the medical college runs on safe AI use. And I'd add a bit more to savings each month, maybe fifty or a hundred extra, just in case contracts change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Interested, but with one eye on the door.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd be one of the most junior. Who would go first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably not anyone outright. More likely, when the two older doctors retire, the partners don't replace them and spread the work using software. Fewer new jobs, not firings, but that still means fewer places for young doctors like me to move to later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who outside the clinic would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ines's mum runs a small bookkeeping business from her kitchen. Bookkeeping is right in the middle of that card. My partner Ines would be the one supporting her mum, and I'd be supporting Ines.

say: I'd say we should **shape the change** with patient safety rules.
I'd want staff to **share the time saved**, and I'd share articles online.
think: I think it's mostly **good for me** in the short run, killing the admin.
I worry the owners **won't replace** retiring doctors, shrinking future jobs.
do: Join the clinic's **AI tools group** once other clinics prove it works.
Do the medical college's short **online course** on safe AI use.
Add **fifty to a hundred** more to savings each month.
feel: He feels **uneasy**, interested but with one eye on the door.
S1.quote: Fewer new jobs, not firings, but that still means fewer places for young doctors like me to move to later.
fieldNote: He sees **fewer new posts** rather than layoffs as the real risk.
His **steady** style shows: he'd join once other clinics prove the tools.
Family exposure matters: his partner's mother does **bookkeeping**.

steps.text: Join the clinic group that chooses AI tools after other clinics test them
Complete the medical college's online course on safe AI use
Add fifty to a hundred a month to savings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need emergency rules, fast. Public money for retraining, rules on who's liable when AI gets it wrong, and a say for health workers. I'd be loud about it in the association and probably on social media too, which isn't like me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think most of my consulting would be done better by the AI within a couple of years. Listening and deciding is thinking work. The hands-on part, examining a belly, stitching a cut, that buys me until about 2031. After that, I honestly don't know what a family doctor is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop the flat plans for now and keep our savings liquid, about four months' worth. I'd learn the AI tools properly, every day, because the doctor who works with it keeps a job longer than the one who doesn't. I'd also join any union or association push for a guaranteed role for doctors in the room.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. A tight feeling in my chest, which is funny, because I'd tell a patient to come in about that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Ines the night you heard?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That we hold off on the flat for a year and see where my contract lands. Teaching is more hands-on than my job, which is odd to say, so my partner might be safer than me for a while. We'd cut the car down to one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd learn the AI every day. Isn't that helping it replace you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe, but not learning it doesn't stop it either. I'd rather be the doctor who knows when the AI is wrong. I've already seen the note-taker invent a medicine name once.

say: I'd call loudly for **emergency rules** on liability and retraining.
I'd speak up in the **association** and online, which isn't like me.
think: I think AI would do most of my **consulting** better within two years.
Hands-on work buys me until **about 2031**, then I don't know.
do: Put the **flat plans** on hold and keep four months of savings liquid.
Use the **AI tools daily** to stay the doctor who spots its mistakes.
Join the push for a **guaranteed role** for doctors in the room.
feel: He feels **anxious**, with a **tight chest** he'd tell a patient to check.
S2.quote: I'd rather be the doctor who knows when the AI is wrong. I've already seen the note-taker invent a medicine name once.
fieldNote: He sees his **thinking work** going first and plans around the 2031 robot gap.
He resolves the replace-yourself worry **pragmatically**: learning is the safer bet.
He'd delay the **flat** and cut to one car, not panic.

steps.text: Put the flat purchase on hold for a year
Use the clinic's AI tools every day and log its mistakes
Join the association campaign for a guaranteed doctor's role
Sell the second car to cut running costs

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we have five years and no excuse to waste them. I'd want the government planning now: retraining money, a role for health workers in deciding how AI is used, and some kind of income guarantee for people whose jobs go. I'd write to our local representative.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think in five years I'd still be a doctor but a different kind. More time checking, explaining and examining, less deciding. The worry is pay. If one doctor plus AI can do the work of three, they won't pay three salaries.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take a part-time diploma in something hands-on, probably sports and musculoskeletal medicine, because I already like it and it's physical. I'd use the AI tools more each year as other clinics show what works. We'd still buy the flat, but a smaller one, so the mortgage isn't scary on a lower salary.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Still anxious, but it feels like I have something to do about it. That helps.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why sports medicine?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I play five-a-side twice a week and half my patients' problems are knees and backs. Feeling a joint and fixing how someone moves is hands-on, and robots come three years after the AI in this picture. Five plus three is eight years of runway, which is a real career change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said pay could drop. How much could you take?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe a quarter less and we'd still be fine, if the flat is small. More than that and I'd be thinking about clinics in other towns.

say: I'd say five years leaves **no excuse** to waste time.
I'd write to our **local representative** about retraining and income guarantees.
think: I think I'd still be a doctor, but doing more **checking and examining**.
My worry is **pay**, if one doctor plus AI replaces three.
do: Start a part-time diploma in **sports medicine**, which is hands-on.
Use the **AI tools more** each year as other clinics prove them.
Buy a **smaller flat** so the mortgage survives a lower salary.
feel: He feels **anxious** but steadier because he has a **plan**.
S3.quote: Five plus three is eight years of runway, which is a real career change.
fieldNote: He does the **arithmetic** of AI first, robots later, and plans from it.
He'd accept **a quarter less** pay but no more without moving.
His progressive views show in calls for an **income guarantee**.

steps.text: Start a part-time diploma in sports and joint medicine
Write to the local representative about retraining money
Buy a smaller flat with a mortgage that fits a lower salary
Add one new AI tool a year once other clinics use it

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift and we should use it properly. Train doctors for the new job now, protect patients, and make sure the gains don't all go to the companies. I'd keep it measured.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'd be fine for most of it. I'll be 37 when it arrives and 40 when the robots come. That's halfway through a career, which is annoying, but with ten years I can set myself up for whatever's left.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on at Millbrook and pick up the AI tools as they become normal. I'd do the sports medicine diploma in a few years rather than now. And we'd buy the flat on the normal plan, and probably have kids around 32 like we said.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but mostly fine. It's far enough away that it's like thinking about my pension.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you change that calm plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If I saw the clinic stop hiring altogether. That's the sign. When nobody's replacing retiring doctors, the clock is running faster than the card says.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you tell young people to train as doctors in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them to train in something with their hands in it. Nursing, physio, surgery. Medicine that's mostly thinking would be a hard thing to start in 2030.

say: I'd say ten years is **a gift** we should use properly.
I'd want the gains shared, not kept by **the companies**.
think: I think I'd be **fine for most** of the decade.
Arriving at **37**, it hits halfway through my career, which is annoying.
do: Carry on at **Millbrook** and adopt AI tools as they become normal.
Do the **sports medicine** diploma in a few years.
Buy the flat and plan **kids around 32**, as before.
feel: He feels mildly **uneasy** but mostly fine, like thinking about a **pension**.
S4.quote: When nobody's replacing retiring doctors, the clock is running faster than the card says.
fieldNote: Ten years lets him keep his **family plans** intact.
He names a clear **warning sign**: the clinic stops hiring.
He'd steer young people toward **hands-on** care roles.

steps.text: Keep working at Millbrook on his current contract
Plan the sports medicine diploma for around 2029
Watch whether the clinic replaces the two retiring doctors

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. Not because I'd be on the street, but because two years is no time to retrain and the flat and the kids would all go on hold. What would help is paid retraining for health workers and a rule that a doctor signs off what the AI decides.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe how the patients would feel. Half my older patients already struggle to book online. Nobody's asking them.

headlineQuote: Teaching is more hands-on than my job, which is odd to say, so my partner might be safer than me for a while.
portrait: Zane is a **27-year-old** family doctor at a nine-doctor clinic in a market town.
He uses an AI note-taker **now and then** and adopts tools once others prove them.
He is **progressive** and wants rules, retraining and shared gains, but stays measured.
His mood moves from **calm** to anxious as the AGI date nears, mostly over pay.
He plans around the **robot gap**, eyeing sports medicine as a hands-on path.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because two years leaves no time to retrain and puts the flat and kids on hold.
whatWouldHelp: A rule that a **doctor signs off** what the AI decides.
